answer: Why the classical route suggests n log n: the classical FFT-style multiplication runs Theta(log n) butterfly levels, and each level has to scan all Theta(n) stored bits. On a tape machine a scan of the stored data costs time linear in the volume (the wiki's tape procedures pay O(V) per push, pop or copy), so Theta(log n) levels of Theta(n) each give Theta(n log n) in total. Where the new algorithm looks for savings: it attacks the two costs named on the Bitebid page, address movement and butterfly arithmetic. (1) Address movement: swapping two disjoint address chunks of u bits on a fixed number of tapes costs O(V u^tau) with tau = 1 - 2^-50 < 1 (Fizokid page), so the movement is cheaper than a full linear pass by a power of the chunk width. (2) Butterfly arithmetic: one round that applies the two-point step on D axes at once is done as one sifigeg pass costing O(V d^lambda') with lambda' < 1, instead of D passes (Sifigeg page; Makevif page). Each saving is only a power below linear, and the margins add up on the Bitebid page to a total time O(n (lg n)^(1-kappa)) with kappa = 2^-182, so a power of log n is saved and n log n is beaten in this model.

reason: Answered with moderate confidence. The high-level story is supported by the quotes: a linear scan per butterfly level gives n log n on a tape, and chunk interchange at O(V u^tau) with tau < 1, together with grouped butterfly rounds at O(V d^lambda') with lambda' < 1, gives a power-of-log saving. I did not verify the exponents, the rank bound s < Wm, or the factorization of the sifigeg step. I opened 7 of the 15 allowed pages (nut, bog, kaf, rut, tiz, mov, pid). The claim that the classical method pays a linear pass per address move is my inference, not stated on the wiki.
